messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Fisherman
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Stranger Interaction: Talking to strangers, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arjun, a 58‑year‑old fisherman of South Asian descent, has lived most of his life on the waters off the Gulf Coast, his days punctuated by the creak of a boat and the rhythm of the tide. In late summer of 2018, when the sea was unusually calm, a sudden collision with a passing cargo ship shattered his routine. The boom of metal, the splash of seawater, and the deafening crash left him clutching a torn piece of hull while his body convulsed in panic. In the minutes that followed, he could not recall the words that should have guided him; he knew the event was there, but he could not find the language to describe it. Since then, every time a stranger approaches his dock or a new face enters his small town, he feels that same surge of terror, as if the memory is pulling him back into the instant of the wreck. These stranger interactions have become potent triggers that, instantly, evoke the visceral image of a car—his fishing vessel—hit by an unseen force, reminding him of the collision and sending the scene back into the present. Arjun’s distrust of others now runs deeper than mere caution. The very act of speaking to strangers, even to a fisherman who offers a friendly nod, feels like a betrayal because he believes people are not what they seem. That belief fuels a heightened sense of threat: the silence that follows a conversation feels like a prelude to danger, and his body, once a reliable tool for hauling nets, now seems deceptive. His constant scanning for danger in the low light of his own home, the way he holds his breath when the wind shifts, is a direct expression of that threat. The belief that his body can no longer be trusted compels him to keep a rigid guard even inside his modest dwelling, and he often finds himself staring at the shadow of a curtain, convinced that a hidden danger lurks. The terror that floods Arjun’s mind whenever he recalls the wreck is almost as intense as the terror he felt at the moment of impact. Each recollection feels present, as if the crash is happening again, and the fear is so profound that he is convinced his life is in imminent peril. This terror on recall is not simply a flashback; it reshapes his sense of self. He no longer recognizes himself, because the identity that once thrived on the ocean’s rhythm is now eclipsed by the image of a shattered hull and a trembling body. That identity loss reinforces his distrust and heightens his perception of threat, creating a loop where every memory of the event feeds back into the cycle of fear and suspicion. When he feels the sting of danger in his own home, the same image of the collision resurfaces, and the memory reasserts its presence, pulling him further into his protective shell. In his current work, Arjun has begun to avoid venturing beyond the familiar reef, steering clear of any vessel that does not match his own. He now refuses to accept passengers on his boat, fearing the strangers who might board could betray him. The constant threat he perceives—whether in the hush of a crowded dock or the quiet of his cabin—makes him retreat from the community that once provided him companionship. The body unreliability he feels has led him to avoid the physical exertions that once defined his identity, and his sense of self erodes further with each missed haul. The memory of the crash, the feeling that it is always present, and the belief that he cannot trust those around him and even his own body have become the scaffolding that supports the relentless threat that governs his day. It is this unrelenting cycle—triggers that summon the memory, memory that stokes negative appraisals, and appraisals that elevate threat—that has driven Arjun to seek help. He has come to believe that without an intervention he will continue to live in a state of constant alert, unable to enjoy the simple peace of his own home or the camaraderie of his fellow fishermen. His most pressing fear is that the memory will never let him rest, that the terror on recall will persist until he loses the one thing that still grounds him: his sense of self and his trust in his own body. Yet he holds a fragile hope that, through understanding and treatment, he might reclaim the voice he lost after the crash and find a way to let the sea’s rhythm flow through him once more.
